User: so here's the argument: ## My argument

The primary cost of off-the-shelf software is **loss of operational flexibility**.

My objection is practical. A prebuilt product can only fit me to the extent that my needs overlap with the needs of the users it was designed around. When my requirements fall outside that overlap, I either have to adapt my way of working to the software or accept that the software cannot do exactly what I need. [...] and here's some research online: ## Position being preserved

* **The central loss from off-the-shelf software is operational flexibility.**

  Your objection is practical. The problem is that the tool cannot be redirected whenever your requirements change, not primarily that the vendor possesses political power, owns the data, or expresses the wrong ideology. [...] * **No position should yet be inferred from your unanswered question 1.3.**

  You have not said whether packaged software actively shapes organizations or merely reflects organizations’ willingness to accept standardization. That issue remains open rather than being folded into your argument.
